title: story
description: An approved story artifact. This schema does not merely check a story, it drives the parse: orchestration/story_parser.py reads a story guided by the node it is at, so items.type of "string" takes a "- " line verbatim (colons included) while items.type of "object" parses the same syntax into key/value pairs. That makes the story dialect NOT YAML — a conforming YAML parser terminates a plain scalar at the first ": " and would read the committed criterion "- A test demonstrates the one-file-edit property: editing only ..." as a mapping rather than a string. Never load a story artifact with yaml.safe_load; the two readings disagree. The coordinator parses with this schema and then validates the result against it before any run state is created.

story.description: Identity and intent of the story.

id.description: Sequential identifier of the form story-NNN.

description.description: What the story changes and why.

workflow.description: Optional. Names the workflow definition under workflows/ this story's run loads, so the choice of workflow is attached to the work item rather than to the target's configuration. Its absence means the run loads the workflow the target configuration names, which is what every artifact written before this field existed does. A name with no definition under workflows/ is refused when the planning session ends and again at pre-flight, and a planning session whose artifact names a workflow other than the one the session was rendered against is refused too, because the planner's stage facts are injected before the interview that would otherwise choose. A resumed run loads the workflow its state.json records rather than re-reading this field.

tasks.description: The discrete units of work the story comprises.

acceptance_criteria.description: Observable conditions the verifier evaluates against.

technical_plan.description: Optional planner-produced implementation guidance. story-001 and story-002 wrote this as a free-form block scalar, before this schema existed; they are execution records rather than inputs and are not held to this contract. See the corpus test in tests/test_story_parser.py.

implementation_steps.description: Ordered steps the implementer is expected to follow.

likely_file_changes.description: Files the plan expects to touch, with the reason for each.

reason.description: Why this file is expected to change.

stage.description: The workflow stage the plan expects to change this file. Advisory only: it tells an agent reading the plan whether an entry is its own work, so a flat unowned list does not read as "your job" to whichever stage looks first. The coordinator never compares this to what a stage actually changed — a prediction that guesses wrong must not end a run. The enforced rule is may_not_create in the workflow definition.

reverting_breaks_the_suite.description: Optional. The planner's judgement that this entry is a test adaptation forced by a deliberate change elsewhere in the same story, so reverting it would break the suite. Its presence is what plan time reads: an entry beneath a prefix its own stage is restricted under, carrying this and naming a path the target root already holds, is accepted without a grant. The text is a judgement for a human reviewer — no check parses, matches or scores it — which is the shape stage_exceptions.reason already has. It is honoured only for a path the target root already holds: an entry naming a path the target lacks describes a creation the ownership check refuses outright, and a claim about reverting a file that does not exist asserts nothing. It is not a grant, and the difference is the point: no run-time check consults it, so the revert check governs a declared path exactly as it governs an undeclared one and adjudicates the claim itself. Where the deliverable is the governed file, a stage_exceptions grant is still the instrument.

scope.description: The boundary the implementer must stay inside.

modify.description: Paths the story is authorized to change.

do_not_modify.description: Paths the story must leave alone.

verification_requirements.description: What the verifier must confirm before the story can pass.

constraints.description: Standing limits on how the story may be implemented.

mandate.description: What conferred the right to run this work, and the whole of what the coordinator resolves before a run creates anything. It is written by the harness process that observed the authorizing act and never by an agent: an artifact that arrives from a planning session already carrying one is refused rather than trusted, on the rule that a required output must be written by the attempt that ran. Observing that act is asking and being answered: l5-plan asks the developer whether they approve the plan once the planning session has ended, and stamps only what the answer gave it, so this block records something the process watched happen rather than something it inferred from a terminal and a file. A rejection stamps nothing, and an artifact carrying a block the session wrote is put to the developer as part of that same question, because approving it discards what the session wrote. A process holding a recorded approval of some other kind confers through the same seam without asking anything. Resolution is a walk — follow source until kind is human — so an absent block, an id that does not resolve, a chain that returns to an id already visited, and a chain longer than the configured mandate_max_depth each refuse the run, and each says which of the four it was. The walk knows no kind but human: what any other kind means is settled by this declaration and by what a lookup can answer for it, never by a condition in the coordinator, which is where workflow selection and history routing already put their own vocabulary. There is deliberately no digest of the artifact's content beside it: the approver and the editor are the same person, an agent editing an approved artifact is closed by blocking the directory it lives in, and a forged block is caught by the record the conferring process writes.

source.description: What the right to run came from. A kind of human terminates the walk in one hop, with no lookup consulted and nothing reached for; every other kind is handed to the lookup, which answers with the mandate that source carries or answers nothing at all — and answering nothing is an id that did not resolve rather than a permission.

kind.description: What conferred the right. The value human is the one the walk recognises, and it is where the walk ends; any other value is resolved through id.

id.description: What a non-human source is resolved through, and what a repeat visit is recognised by. Absent for a source whose kind is human, because a human is where the walk ends and there is nothing further to follow.

conferred_at.description: When the authorizing act was observed, in the YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json already use. Read by nothing that routes; it is what makes the record answerable later.

conferred_by.description: The identity the authorizing act was observed from, taken by the conferring process from the target repository's own git identity. It is what a resolved walk terminates at and what the run's evidence names.

recorded_by.description: The harness process that observed the act and wrote this block. It is not the agent that wrote the body around it, and it is never one: a block naming a stage, a prompt or a planning agent is a block nothing observed.

stage_exceptions.description: Optional, and rare: explicit grants lifting a stage's may_not_create declaration for this story only. A granted path is one the story declares that stage owns, so neither the ownership check nor the revert check governs it and the reviewer weighs the reason instead — which is why the reason is required: the grant is a judgement, not a flag. A story whose deliverable is itself a regression suite needs the implementer's tests/ restriction lifted. Not in the top-level required list — almost every story declares none. The coordinator cross-checks each entry against the loaded workflow at pre-flight and refuses a grant that names an undefined stage or a value beneath no prefix that stage was restricted on.

stage.description: Name of the workflow stage the grant applies to.

create.description: A repository-relative path that stage may write, and it must be a value one of that stage's own path restrictions governs — which is the same question the ownership check and the revert check ask of a path, so a grant lifts exactly what those checks would otherwise decide. Under a may_not_create declaration that means a value at or beneath one of the prefixes it names; under a may_only_change declaration it means a value outside every prefix it names, which is where that stage's writes are governed. Naming the whole prefix exempts everything beneath it, exactly as it always has; naming a single file exempts that file alone, leaving every other path that restriction governs governed. A value ending in a slash is read as a directory and covers every path beneath it; any other value covers exactly and only itself. A value no restriction on that stage governs is refused, because it grants nothing.

reason.description: Why this story needs the rule lifted.
